nameStory: This charming beetle earned its 'spotted pink lady' name from its delicate pink coloration adorned with distinctive black spots - a softer, more feminine appearance than the classic red ladybug we all know. The 'pink lady' part distinguishes it from other spotted lady beetles, giving this species its own special identity in the diverse ladybug family.
description: The Spotted Pink Lady Beetle is a beneficial garden insect that looks like a gentler cousin of the classic red ladybug. These beetles display a lovely pink to pale orange coloration with prominent black spots scattered across their wing covers. They're among the larger lady beetles you'll encounter in New England, with a distinctly oval, dome-shaped body. Like other lady beetles, they're voracious predators of garden pests, especially aphids.

idTips.label: Pink coloration
idTips.description: The wing covers (elytra) are distinctly pink to pale orange rather than the bright red of common ladybugs - they have a soft, almost pastel appearance that catches the eye

idTips.label: Black spots
idTips.description: Usually displays 12 black spots arranged across the wing covers, though the number can vary slightly - the spots are clearly defined and contrasting against the pink background

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: Noticeably larger than many other lady beetles, with a distinctly oval, dome-shaped body that feels smooth and hard when gently touched

idTips.label: Head and pronotum
idTips.description: The head and the shield-like area behind it (pronotum) are typically black or very dark, creating a stark contrast with the pink wing covers

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often found actively hunting aphids on plant stems and leaves, moving with deliberate, methodical movements rather than quick scurrying

habitat: Spotted Pink Lady Beetles thrive in gardens, agricultural areas, and edge habitats throughout New England where aphids are abundant. You'll find them on a wide variety of plants including crops, ornamental flowers, and wild plants in fields and meadows. They prefer sunny, open areas with diverse plant communities that support healthy aphid populations for hunting.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hiding spots and begin actively hunting aphids on early spring plants. This is when you're most likely to see them moving deliberately across plant stems.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible, actively feeding and mating. Look for them on garden plants and agricultural crops during warm, sunny days.
seasonality.fall: Adults prepare for winter by feeding heavily and seeking shelter under leaf litter, bark, or rocks. They may still be active on warm autumn days.
seasonality.winter: Adults hibernate in protected locations like under rocks, logs, or leaf litter. Occasionally emerge on unusually warm winter days but generally remain dormant.

funFact: Despite being called a 'lady beetle,' these pink beauties are actually voracious predators that can consume up to 5,000 aphids in their lifetime - making them one of a gardener's most valuable allies in natural pest control!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other lady beetles, but the distinctive pink coloration makes identification relatively easy - if it's pink with black spots, it's likely this species. Remember: 'Pink ladies are unique ladies' - no other common New England lady beetle sports this soft pink hue.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'twelve-spotted lady beetle' is sometimes used for this species, but this can be confusing since spot counts can vary and other species may also have twelve spots. The 'spotted pink lady beetle' name helps avoid this confusion by emphasizing the distinctive pink coloration that truly sets this species apart.
compareHints: Since this is the only Coleomegilla species in New England, compare it with other common lady beetles in the Coccinellidae family. The pink coloration immediately separates it from the bright red Seven-spot Lady Beetle or the variable Asian Lady Beetle. Even when Asian Lady Beetles appear orange or pale, they lack the distinctive soft pink hue and typically have different spot patterns.
